strengths: Addresses an important deployment bottleneck with a coherent algorithm-system co-design. Speculative retrieval, head-wise correction, hybrid CPU/GPU layouts, and streamed recall fit together naturally.
The group-consistent selection design is practically relevant for GQA models, and the proposed one-step reuse mechanism offers a plausible way to move retrieval off the critical path.

Accuracy evaluation is relatively broad, covering six model variants and long-input, long-generation, mathematical-reasoning, and domain-reasoning tasks. Comparisons include representative static dropping, dynamic dropping, and retrieval baselines.

The end-to-end latency results on an A100 show substantial gains over offloaded retrieval baselines. The efficiency ablation also usefully indicates that hybrid layouts provide most of the improvement, with double buffering and speculative retrieval adding further gains.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and provides intuitive diagrams of both the algorithmic schedule and memory layout.
weaknesses: The central proxy underlying fine-grained correction is insufficiently validated. High cosine similarity between adjacent queries does not necessarily imply high overlap among top-ranked pages. The paper does not report correlation with retrieval-set overlap, correction precision/recall, correction frequency, attention-output error, or failure cases.

Important accuracy-efficiency ablations are missing: there is no isolated accuracy effect of speculative reuse, correction, group pooling, or page summaries, and no sensitivity analysis for the correction threshold, cache budget, page size, sequence length, or sink/window sizes. Consequently, the claimed Pareto improvement is supported only at a few hand-selected operating points.

The system comparison is not reproducible or demonstrably controlled. Framework and kernel versions, baseline integration details, timing methodology, warmup/repetition counts, and variance are omitted. Several baselines are materially modified, while it is unclear whether the dominant hybrid-layout optimization was applied to them; this makes attribution of the large speedups difficult.

The claimed O(B) GPU-memory complexity appears to omit page summaries and associated metadata retained on the GPU, which scale with context length. No measured peak-memory results are provided, despite memory scalability being a central motivation.

Stochastic reasoning results use relatively small problem subsets and provide no confidence intervals or paired significance tests. LongGenBench additionally relies on a single LLM judge without judge-validation or uncertainty analysis, so small reported differences should not be interpreted strongly.

The individual ingredients—one-step temporal reuse, threshold-based correction, layout conversion, and double buffering—are fairly incremental. The positioning against prior temporal KV/attention sharing is brief, and the paper does not clearly establish which components are technically novel beyond their integration.

Efficiency is evaluated on only one older GPU/CPU platform and two 7B–8B models, without throughput, multi-request serving, newer interconnects, or larger-model measurements. This limits support for broad deployment claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important systems problem: retaining the accuracy advantages of recallable KV-cache compression while reducing selection and CPU–GPU transfer overhead.

The proposed design is coherent across algorithm and system layers. Speculative retrieval, head-wise correction, hybrid CPU/GPU layouts, and double-buffered recall fit together naturally and are explained with useful diagrams.

The accuracy study covers several model families and three distinct regimes: long-input understanding, long-form generation, and long reasoning. FreeKV is generally close to the full-KV results and often stronger than the compression baselines.

The reported end-to-end gains are potentially substantial, reaching 13.7× over ArkVale, and the efficiency ablation provides some evidence that hybrid layouts, streamed recall, and speculative retrieval each contribute.
weaknesses: The central premise is insufficiently validated. High cosine similarity between adjacent queries does not necessarily imply substantial overlap between the top-ranked KV pages. The paper reports mean query similarity for limited examples but does not measure page-selection overlap, missed attention mass, correction frequency, or how these quantities predict accuracy.

Critical algorithmic ablations are missing. There is no accuracy–latency sweep over the correction threshold, no comparison of pure reuse against reuse with correction, and no sensitivity analysis for page size, retrieval budget, sink size, or local-window size. Consequently, it is unclear whether the chosen task-specific hyperparameters were tuned on the evaluation sets or how robust the method is.

The systems evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the efficiency claims. It uses one A100 PCIe platform, only two roughly 7–8B models, two fixed workload shapes, and batch sizes up to four. It does not report throughput, per-token latency, peak GPU/CPU memory, transfer bandwidth, correction rates, profiling timelines, variance across runs, or comparisons on newer accelerators and interconnects.

The efficiency comparison is incomplete. Quest and a full-KV baseline are absent from the end-to-end latency figure, despite being important reference points elsewhere in the paper. There is also insufficient information about kernel implementations, framework versions, compilation settings, warm-up, number of repetitions, and whether all baselines received comparable optimization effort.

Several baselines are materially modified: Quest and RaaS are changed to enforce group-consistent selection, while ShadowKV is extended with periodic SVD updates. The paper does not validate these adaptations against the original implementations or isolate their accuracy and runtime effects, making the fairness and reproducibility of the comparison difficult to assess.

The stochastic accuracy experiments are statistically underpowered and lack uncertainty estimates. Reasoning evaluation uses only 50 examples for MATH500 and GPQA, while LongGenBench relies on an LLM judge; no confidence intervals, significance tests, judge-validation analysis, or run-to-run variability are reported. Small apparent improvements over full KV therefore should not be interpreted as evidence of superior accuracy.

The claimed near-lossless behavior is supported only at a single budget of 2048 and task-dependent settings. The paper does not establish the accuracy–memory–latency Pareto frontier across budgets, even though this trade-off is fundamental to KV-cache compression.

Reproducibility is weak: the manuscript provides no code or artifact statement, detailed pseudocode, kernel-level implementation details, or sufficient instructions to reproduce the scheduling and synchronization behavior. Overall, the idea is promising, but the missing validation and incomplete systems methodology prevent the current evidence from meeting a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: FreeKV presents a clear, practically important algorithm-system co-design for reducing the substantial selection and CPU-GPU recall overhead of retrieval-based KV-cache compression.
The combination of speculative one-step KV reuse, head-wise correction, hybrid CPU/GPU layouts, and double-buffered streamed recall is coherent and technically well motivated.

The evaluation covers long-input, long-generation, and long-reasoning workloads across six model configurations, with comparisons against representative static dropping, dynamic dropping, and retrieval baselines.

Accuracy is generally close to full-KV inference, while the reported efficiency gains are substantial: up to 13.7x over ArkVale and 8.4x over ShadowKV, with performance approaching cheaper dropping methods.

The paper is well organized, and its diagrams effectively explain the execution timeline and data-layout optimizations. weaknesses: The key algorithmic premise is not validated deeply enough: high cosine similarity between adjacent queries does not necessarily imply substantial overlap between selected KV pages. Direct measurements of selection overlap, threshold precision/recall, and correction frequency are missing.

There is no accuracy-focused ablation isolating speculative reuse and fine-grained correction, nor a systematic budget/threshold sensitivity study. Consequently, the claimed accuracy-efficiency trade-off and the necessity of the correction design are insufficiently characterized.

Efficiency experiments are restricted to one A100 PCIe system and two 7B/8B models. Results across other interconnects, GPUs, larger models, longer input contexts, and serving-oriented throughput or concurrency settings would strengthen the systems claims.

Baseline fairness is somewhat difficult to assess because RaaS, Quest, and ShadowKV are modified from their original implementations. The paper does not quantify how these modifications affect either accuracy or efficiency, and equal token budgets do not necessarily imply equal memory use or comparable implementation quality.

The reasoning evaluation uses only 50 sampled MATH500 questions, 50 GPQA questions, and 30 AIME24 questions. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported, so several small apparent improvements over full KV or competing methods may reflect sampling variance.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of code or sufficiently detailed implementation information, including kernel design, synchronization behavior, cache-management policy, initialization handling, and exact per-baseline integration details.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in long-context LLM inference and presents a coherent algorithm-system co-design: speculative retrieval and selective correction are paired with hybrid CPU/GPU layouts and double-buffered recall.

The core empirical observation—high adjacent-step query similarity—is examined across several tasks, model sizes, architectures, and training stages, providing reasonable motivation for speculative reuse.
The evaluation is unusually broad in task coverage, including long-input understanding, long-form generation, and mathematical/scientific reasoning across multiple Llama and Qwen-family models.

Comparisons include several relevant KV-dropping and KV-retrieval baselines. Reported accuracy is generally close to full-cache inference, while end-to-end latency improvements over retrieval baselines are large, especially for long generation and larger batches.

Ablations study selection aggregation, correction policy and threshold, input/output lengths, and the contributions of hybrid layouts, double buffering, and speculative retrieval. The correction-rate analysis is also useful for understanding workload dependence.
The method is training-free and supports long generation with a fixed retrieved-KV budget, making the contribution practically relevant.
weaknesses: The claimed O(B) GPU-memory complexity is misleading because FreeKV retains page summaries for the complete context on the GPU; this component grows with context length. The paper should report exact peak GPU and CPU memory, including summaries, buffers, metadata, and cached pages, rather than only asymptotic selected-KV storage.

The efficiency evidence is limited to one A100/PCIe platform and two roughly 7–8B models. Results may change substantially with H100-class GPUs, NVLink, different CPU bandwidths, larger models, or concurrent serving. Throughput, time-to-first-token, peak memory, host bandwidth, and multi-request scheduling results are absent.

The ablation indicates that hybrid layout alone supplies most of the speedup—up to 10.5x—while speculative retrieval adds a smaller gain. This weakens the framing of speculative retrieval as the principal enabler and calls for clearer attribution of headline speedups.

Baseline fairness is difficult to assess because several baselines are materially modified to enforce group-consistent selection, and ShadowKV is extended with periodic SVD updates. The paper does not show that these adaptations preserve each baseline's best accuracy-efficiency trade-off or clearly account for all update costs.

Query cosine similarity does not necessarily imply overlap of selected pages or bounded attention-output error. The paper provides no direct measurements of retrieval-set overlap, missed attention mass, or error versus similarity, so the correction criterion remains heuristic and its failure modes are insufficiently characterized.

Accuracy differences are often small relative to the limited evaluation samples, but no confidence intervals, variance across seeds, or significance tests are reported. The reasoning evaluation uses only 50 MATH500 and 50 GPQA questions, and LongGenBench relies on a single Qwen-3-32B judge without reporting judge prompts or validation.

The 'full latency hiding' claim is stronger than the presented evidence. There is no detailed trace or latency breakdown for FreeKV itself showing residual selection/recall stalls, particularly on hard tasks where correction rates reach 0.43–0.52.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript says code is available but the displayed footnote lacks a usable repository link, and important implementation details—kernel configuration, synchronization, cache-management costs, measurement protocol, warm-up, and variance—are missing.

The evaluation fixes the retrieval budget at 2048 and tunes the correction threshold by scenario, but does not present accuracy-latency Pareto curves over budgets and thresholds. Consequently, robustness under tighter memory budgets and the practical cost of threshold selection remain unclear.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck in long-context LLM inference with a coherent algorithm-system co-design.
Speculative retrieval with selective correction is intuitive, training-free, and supported by query-similarity measurements across several model families, scales, tasks, and training stages.
The hybrid CPU/GPU layouts and double-buffered streamed recall are technically sensible, and the component ablation attributes substantial latency gains to these optimizations.
Accuracy experiments cover long-input, long-generation, and reasoning workloads, with comparisons against multiple recent KV-dropping and KV-retrieval methods.
Reported end-to-end speedups are large, reaching 13.7x over ArkVale while retaining accuracy close to full-KV inference in the tested settings.
weaknesses: The central efficiency evidence is too narrow: all latency results use one A100 PCIe system, only two 7B-8B models, and batch sizes up to four. There is no evaluation on newer accelerators, other interconnects, larger models, or multi-GPU serving.

Efficiency is not evaluated on the hard reasoning workloads where correction rates reach 43-52%. Since correction places selection and recall back on the critical path, the headline full-overlap and speedup claims may not hold precisely where correction is most needed.

Baseline fairness is difficult to establish. Several competitors are modified to enforce group consistency or support long generation, yet the effects of these modifications on their original accuracy and performance are not isolated. Quest is also omitted from latency comparisons.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates, repeated-run variation, and statistical tests. Reasoning experiments use only 50 MATH500 and 50 GPQA questions, while many reported differences are small and can plausibly arise from stochastic decoding.

The claimed near-lossless behavior is not demonstrated across budget or compression-ratio sweeps. Results use a single retrieval budget of 2048, task-specific thresholds, and LongBench inputs truncated to 64K despite the paper's motivation involving contexts up to 1M-2M tokens.

Query cosine similarity is only an indirect proxy for overlap between selected KV pages. The paper provides no analysis of retrieval-set overlap, missed attention mass, or cases where high query similarity nevertheless changes the top pages.

Important deployment measurements are missing, including peak CPU/GPU memory, transfer volume, throughput under concurrent requests, and comparison with full-KV or standard inference engines. Figure 7 also provides no error bars or detailed timing protocol.

The novelty is moderate: previous-step reuse is a simple speculation heuristic, while hybrid layouts and double buffering are established systems techniques. The contribution lies mainly in their integration rather than a fundamentally new principle.

Reproducibility is currently limited: the manuscript says code is available but provides no accessible repository or artifact, and it omits enough implementation and benchmarking detail to make the large speedups difficult to independently verify.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck in long-context LLM inference with a coherent algorithm-system co-design: speculative retrieval and selective correction are paired effectively with hybrid CPU/GPU layouts and double-buffered streamed recall.
The central empirical result is compelling: FreeKV substantially reduces end-to-end latency—up to 13.7× versus ArkVale—while remaining competitive with efficient KV-dropping methods.

Accuracy evaluation is unusually broad, covering long-input, long-generation, and reasoning workloads across several Llama- and Qwen-family models. FreeKV is generally close to full-KV inference and competitive with or better than the retrieval baselines.

The paper includes useful ablations for correction thresholds, group-consistent selection and correction, query-source choice, hybrid layouts, double buffering, and speculative retrieval. The query-similarity and correction-rate analyses also help explain when the method works.
The presentation is clear and technically well motivated, and the method is training-free with bounded GPU KV-cache memory, increasing its practical relevance.
weaknesses: Efficiency is evaluated on only one hardware configuration—an A100 connected through PCIe Gen4—and primarily two 7B/8B models. Results across other accelerators, interconnects, CPU platforms, and larger models are needed to establish that the overlap and speedups generalize.

The baseline comparison is not fully clean: several baselines are modified to enforce group consistency, ShadowKV is extended with periodic SVD updates, and Quest is excluded from efficiency experiments. More implementation details and validation against original baseline numbers are needed to rule out engineering-quality differences.

High cosine similarity between adjacent queries does not by itself establish stability of the selected top pages. Direct measurements of page-set overlap, missed attention mass, and their relationship to the correction criterion would support the algorithmic premise more convincingly.

The accuracy evidence lacks uncertainty estimates or statistical tests. This matters especially for the reasoning experiments, which use only 50 MATH500 and GPQA questions, and for LongGenBench, which relies on a single LLM judge; several apparent gains over full KV inference may simply reflect sampling variance.

The correction threshold is task-regime dependent and correction rates reach 0.47–0.52 on difficult reasoning tasks. The paper does not fully characterize worst-case latency, sensitivity under distribution shift, or an automatic policy for choosing the threshold.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: the claimed code link is missing or malformed, and low-level implementation details sufficient to reproduce the asynchronous scheduling and optimized baselines are limited. These weaknesses keep the paper at a marginal accept rather than a clear accept.
